::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 1"}
Here's how to get set up in RStudio.

#### 1. Create the R Markdown file

- **File → New File → R Markdown…**, give it a title, choose HTML (or PDF/Word) output, and click OK.
- Save the `.Rmd` in the same folder as `colectomy-data.csv`. R Markdown knits relative to the file's own folder, so `read.csv("colectomy-data.csv")` will work without a full path.
- Delete the template content below the YAML header (the block between the `---` lines).

#### 2. Packages that are useful for an ANCOVA workflow

None of these are strictly required, since base R can fit the model with `lm()`. They make the work easier, though:

| Package | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `tidyverse` | Reading data (`read_csv`), wrangling (`dplyr`), plotting (`ggplot2`) |
| `car` | `Anova()` for Type II/III sums of squares, `leveneTest()`, `vif()` |
| `emmeans` | Adjusted (estimated marginal) means and contrasts with CIs |
| `effectsize` | Effect sizes such as partial $\eta^2$ |
| `performance` | `check_model()`, a quick panel of assumption-check plots |
| `knitr` | `kable()` for clean tables in the knitted report |

Install them once from the console, not inside the Rmd:

```r
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "car", "emmeans", "effectsize", "performance", "knitr"))
```

#### 3. Setup chunk at the top of your Rmd

````markdown
```{{r setup, include=FALSE}}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(car)
library(emmeans)
library(effectsize)
library(performance)
library(knitr)
```
````

#### 4. Read the data and set factor types

````markdown
```{{r load-data}}
dat <- read_csv("colectomy-data.csv")
str(dat)
summary(dat)
```
````

`read_csv` will read `approach` and `diabetes` as character columns. You'll want to convert them to factors with `factor()`. If you want a particular group as the reference level, you can set it with the `levels =` argument.

#### 5. Outline your sections

It may help to add headers that mirror the required report sections: Design, Method & Justification, Variable Selection, Assumption Checks, Results, and Interpretation. That way you can fill them in as you go.

Which variables go into the model, and why, is your call to make and justify in the report. Once you've decided and written some code, paste your code or output here and I can help with syntax, errors, or reading the output.
:::

They're useful, and two of them you already have through the tidyverse:

- **`dplyr`** is data wrangling: `filter()`, `select()`, `mutate()` (e.g., converting columns to factors), `group_by()` + `summarise()` for group descriptives. It's loaded automatically by `library(tidyverse)`.
- **`ggplot2`** is the plotting system: boxplots, scatterplots, histograms, Q-Q plots. It's also part of the tidyverse, so it's loaded automatically too.
- **`ggpubr`** is not part of the tidyverse. It's a wrapper around ggplot2 that makes publication-style plots quickly, with functions like `ggboxplot()`, `ggscatter()`, `ggqqplot()`, `ggdensity()`, and it can add p-values or regression lines to plots. It's handy if you'd rather not build plots layer by layer.

So in your setup chunk, `library(tidyverse)` covers dplyr and ggplot2. Just add:

```r
library(ggpubr)
```

A quick example of each style, so you can see the difference:

```r
ggplot(dat, aes(x = approach, y = qor15_30d)) + geom_boxplot()

ggboxplot(dat, x = "approach", y = "qor15_30d")
```

Both give the same kind of plot, so use whichever feels more comfortable.

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 5"}
Yes, **Knit** is how you see the full rendered document, but there are a couple of ways to view things as you go.

**1. Run chunks interactively (fastest while working)**

- Click the green ▶ arrow at the top-right of a chunk, or press **Ctrl+Shift+Enter** (Cmd+Shift+Enter on Mac), to run that chunk.
- **Ctrl+Enter** runs just the current line or selection.
- Output appears right under the chunk in the editor. If you'd rather see it in the Console and Plots pane, click the gear ⚙ next to Knit and choose **"Chunk Output in Console."**
- Objects you create this way show up in the **Environment** pane, so later chunks can use them.

**2. Knit (the full rendered report)**

- Click **Knit** at the top of the editor, or press **Ctrl+Shift+K**.
- This runs the whole document from scratch in a clean session and produces the HTML, PDF, or Word file, which opens in a viewer window or the Viewer pane.
- To have it show in the Viewer pane instead of a popup, go to the gear ⚙ → **"Preview in Viewer Pane."**

**One gotcha:** knitting does *not* use your Environment. If something works when you run chunks interactively but fails on knit, it's usually because a package is loaded, or a variable is created, somewhere other than in the Rmd itself, or the chunks are out of order. Everything the report needs has to be in the file, top to bottom.

A good rhythm is to run chunks interactively while you're building and knit every so often to make sure the whole thing still renders cleanly.
:::

Good start. Here's how to convert those two columns. You can put this right after `read_csv()` in your `load-data` chunk, or in its own chunk:

```r
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    approach = factor(approach),
    diabetes = factor(diabetes)
  )

str(dat)  # confirm they now show as Factor
```

By default, `factor()` orders levels alphabetically, so `Laparoscopic` will be the reference level for `approach` and `No` for `diabetes`. If you want a different reference group, set the order explicitly. The first level listed becomes the reference:

```r
approach = factor(approach, levels = c("Open", "Laparoscopic"))
```

The reference level matters mainly for how you read the coefficients later. The approach coefficient will be "the other group minus the reference group," so pick whichever direction you find most natural to interpret.

You can check the levels with:

```r
levels(dat$approach)
table(dat$approach)
```

One small tip: if you run `str(dat)` and `summary(dat)` *after* the conversion, the summary will show counts per level for the factors instead of just "character," which is more informative for your report.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 19"}
Your list covers the core assumptions. A few additions and one clarification:

**Your list:**

1. **Independence of observations**, which you argue from the design.
2. **Linearity** between each continuous covariate and the outcome.
3. **Homogeneity of regression slopes:** yes, you test this with interaction terms.
4. **Normality of residuals.**
5. **Homogeneity of variance**, which concerns the variance of the *outcome residuals* across groups. The table you made shows SDs of age and BMI, which are covariates, so it doesn't speak to this assumption. You'll still want to check it separately.

**Commonly added:**

6. **Covariates independent of the treatment.** Often argued from randomization, and you can point to your balance table.
7. **Outliers and influential points**, which aren't strictly an assumption but are part of a standard check.
8. **Multicollinearity among predictors**, if you have several covariates. `vif()` from `car` checks this.

**How to check each one in R.** Replace the right-hand side with whatever model you choose:

```r
fit <- lm(qor15_30d ~ approach + covariate1 + covariate2, data = dat)

fit_int <- lm(qor15_30d ~ approach * covariate1 + approach * covariate2, data = dat)
Anova(fit_int, type = 3)        # look at the interaction rows
anova(fit, fit_int)

ggscatter(dat, x = "covariate1", y = "qor15_30d", color = "approach",
          add = "reg.line")

res <- residuals(fit)
ggqqplot(res)
shapiro.test(res)

leveneTest(res ~ approach, data = dat)

vif(fit)

check_model(fit)
```

For the slopes check, a non-significant interaction is consistent with equal slopes. For Levene's test and Shapiro-Wilk, a non-significant p-value means no evidence of a violation. With $n = 200$, Shapiro-Wilk can flag trivial departures, so many people lean on the Q-Q plot as the primary evidence.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="User · turn 20"}
Actually, going on a tiny bit of a tangent here, but covariates being independent from treatment, how is that actually handled irl? I mean, we can certainly point to our balance table in this case and say that the covariates have been divided up equally, but that feels a little weird. The covariates being independent from the treatment is given by the randomization, but we can still theoretically randomize the treatment and get highly unequal balance. How is that handled? It feels hacky if we were to say "Oh, we looked at the balance table and didn't like the distribution, so we rerandomized". Do you just bite the bullet and say "we had unequal balance, but that's due to random chance in the randomization process, so we continue on regardless"
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 21"}
Your instinct is right on both counts, and this is a well-studied question.

**What randomization actually guarantees**

Randomization makes covariates independent of treatment *in expectation*, over all possible randomizations. Any single realized allocation can be imbalanced by chance. The key point is that this chance imbalance is already accounted for in the inference: p-values and confidence intervals are calibrated over the randomization distribution, which includes the unlucky allocations. So "we had some imbalance by chance, and we proceed" is the textbook-correct stance, not biting a bullet.

**Why significance-testing balance is discouraged**

Many trials used to report p-values comparing baseline characteristics between arms. CONSORT and most methodologists now advise against this. If randomization was done properly, the null hypothesis is *true by construction*, so any "significant" difference is by definition a false positive. A descriptive table (means, SDs, percentages) is the recommended way to report balance. Then you judge whether any difference is large enough to matter *clinically*, not statistically.

**How imbalance is handled in practice**

- **Pre-specified covariate adjustment.** This is the main tool, and it's what ANCOVA does. Adjusting for prognostic baseline covariates corrects for chance imbalance in them and usually tightens the confidence interval. The important part is choosing covariates *in advance*, based on prior knowledge of what predicts the outcome, not after looking at which ones came out imbalanced. Choosing adjustment variables based on observed imbalance opens the door to analytic flexibility.
- **Design-stage fixes**, done before allocation:
  - **Stratified (blocked) randomization:** randomize separately within strata, e.g., diabetic and non-diabetic patients, so those groups are balanced by design.
  - **Minimization:** each new patient is allocated, partly at random, to whichever arm best preserves balance across several factors. It's common in smaller trials.
  - **Rerandomization:** your "hacky" idea is actually a legitimate method (Morgan & Rubin, 2012), *if* the acceptance rule is specified in advance (e.g., "redraw until the Mahalanobis distance between arms is below threshold $a$"), and the analysis accounts for the restricted set of allowable allocations. What's hacky is doing it ad hoc and then analyzing as if it were simple randomization.

**Summary:** randomize once (or with a pre-specified restriction), report balance descriptively, adjust for pre-specified prognostic covariates, and don't let the observed balance drive the analysis choices.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="User · turn 22"}
Oh, how do I do a numbered list in RMarkdown?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 23"}
Same as regular Markdown: start each line with a number and a period, with a blank line before the list.

```markdown
Some text before the list.

1. First item
2. Second item
3. Third item
```

A few details:

- **The numbers don't have to be correct.** Markdown renumbers automatically, so `1.` `1.` `1.` still renders as 1, 2, 3. That makes reordering easy.
- **Blank line before the list:** if the list comes right after a paragraph with no blank line, it may render as plain text instead of a list. This is the most common gotcha.
- **Nested items:** indent by 4 spaces (or a tab).

  ```markdown
  1. Independence
  2. Linearity
      - checked with scatterplots
      - by group
  3. Equal slopes
  ```

- **Bullets** work the same way with `-` or `*` instead of numbers.
:::

I'm not really sure how to interpret this for linearity. I mean, it's not super highly linear, but it's also not obviously nonlinear. It's just kinda a big mess? Are big messes linear?

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 27"}
Big messes can be linear. Linearity is about the **shape** of the average relationship, not how tightly the points cluster around it.

- **Scatter (noise)** is about the *strength* of the relationship. A lot of spread just means the covariate explains a modest share of the variation, which is fine for ANCOVA.
- **Linearity** asks whether the *trend* through the cloud is a straight line or something curved, like a U-shape, a plateau, or a bend. A violation looks like points systematically above the line at both ends and below it in the middle, or similar.

So the question to ask of a plot is: *is there any curvature in the middle of the cloud that a straight line misses?* not *are the points close to the line?*

**Two things that make this easier to judge**

1. **Add a smoother.** A loess curve follows the data without forcing a straight line. If it roughly tracks the straight line, linearity is reasonable; if it bends clearly, that's a concern.

   ```r
   ggplot(dat, aes(x = age, y = qor15_30d, color = approach)) +
     geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
     geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
     geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed")
   ```

2. **Check the residuals from the fitted model**, which is often clearer than raw scatterplots:

   ```r
   crPlots(fit)                  # component + residual plots (car), one per covariate
   plot(fit, which = 1)          # residuals vs fitted; look for a curve in the red line
   ```

   In `crPlots`, the dashed line is the linear fit and the solid line is a smoother. Ideally they roughly overlap.

**About diabetes:** linearity only applies to *continuous* covariates. Diabetes is a two-level factor, so the model just estimates a shift between No and Yes, and there's no "shape" to check. That third plot is better read as a look at how the outcome distributions differ by diabetes status and approach. For a categorical covariate, the relevant check is the interaction (equal-slopes) test, `approach * diabetes`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 29"}
That's a reasonable thing to wonder about, and there's a known reason loess curves misbehave at the edges.

**Why the ends of a loess curve are unreliable**

- **Few points:** at the extremes of the x-axis there's little data, so the smoother is fitting just a handful of points. A few high or low observations can pull it sharply.
- **One-sided neighborhoods:** in the middle, loess averages points on both sides of each x value. At the edges it only has points on one side, which makes it more prone to swooping.

The red curve's swoop on the left is driven by roughly the youngest 4 or 5 Laparoscopic patients. Wiggles in sparse regions are usually given much less weight than a consistent bend through the bulk of the data.

**Two ways to make the judgment less eyeball-dependent**

1. **Show the uncertainty band.** If the straight line sits inside the loess band, the curve isn't distinguishable from linear:

   ```r
   ggplot(dat, aes(x = age, y = qor15_30d, color = approach)) +
     geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
     geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
     geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, linetype = "dashed")
   ```

2. **A formal check:** add a squared term and see if it contributes anything. For a centered quadratic in age:

   ```r
   fit_quad <- lm(qor15_30d ~ approach + age + I((age - mean(age))^2) + ..., data = dat)
   anova(fit, fit_quad)
   ```

   Replace `...` with the rest of your chosen model. A non-significant result means no evidence that curvature improves the fit.

Whether you conclude linearity is adequate is your call. Either way, in the report you can describe what you saw ("the loess curve deviates at low ages, where few observations are present") and what you did about it. Showing that you noticed and checked is the kind of thing that makes an assumptions section convincing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 31"}
You *can* include it. `lm()` handles factor covariates fine, and an ANCOVA model can mix continuous and categorical covariates. Whether diabetes *should* be in the model is your variable-selection decision. The linearity rule doesn't settle it either way, since linearity only concerns how continuous covariates enter the model, not which covariates you include.

Mechanically, here's what happens if you include it:

```r
fit <- lm(qor15_30d ~ approach + age + bmi + diabetes, data = dat)
```

R automatically creates an indicator for the non-reference level, so the coefficient `diabetesYes` is the adjusted difference in mean QoR-15 for patients with diabetes vs. without, holding the other terms constant.

For the quadratic linearity check, you'd add the squared term only for the **continuous** covariate you're testing. Diabetes stays in as-is:

```r
fit_quad <- lm(qor15_30d ~ approach + age + I((age - mean(age))^2) + bmi + diabetes,
               data = dat)
anova(fit, fit_quad)
```

You can't square a two-level factor, and there's no curvature to test. The same applies to the other assumption checks: diabetes goes into the equal-slopes test (`approach * diabetes`), but not into linearity.

The important thing is that `fit` and `fit_quad` contain the same terms apart from the squared one, so that `anova()` is comparing like with like.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 35"}
Your readings of the interaction rows and the Shapiro-Wilk test are right. Before going further, though, there's a **code issue** to fix, because it affects several of these results.

#### Your `fit` doesn't include diabetes

Look at Model 1 in the comparison:

```
Model 1: qor15_30d ~ approach + age + bmi
```

The `vif()` output also lists only `approach`, `age`, `bmi`. So the `fit` object currently in your session was fitted without `diabetes`, probably from an earlier run before you added it. That has two consequences:

1. **The `anova(fit, fit_int)` comparison is invalid as an equal-slopes test.** It's testing 4 extra terms at once (the `diabetes` main effect *plus* the three interactions), so the significant $p = 0.0048$ can't be read as evidence of unequal slopes. For a clean comparison, the two models should differ *only* in the interaction terms.
2. **The Shapiro-Wilk, Levene, and VIF results came from the model without diabetes.** `res` was computed from that `fit`.

The fix is to refit and rerun everything downstream:

```r
fit <- lm(qor15_30d ~ approach + age + bmi + diabetes, data = dat)
fit_int <- lm(qor15_30d ~ approach * age + approach * bmi + approach * diabetes, data = dat)

anova(fit, fit_int)            # now a 3-df test of just the interactions
res <- residuals(fit)
shapiro.test(res)
leveneTest(res ~ approach, data = dat)
vif(fit)
```

The Type III table with the interaction rows is fine as it is, since that came from `fit_int`, which already includes diabetes. The re-run results may change, including Levene's.

#### If unequal variance holds up after refitting

You're right that weighting is an option. The common approaches are:

**1. Heteroskedasticity-consistent (robust) standard errors.** Keep the same coefficients but compute standard errors that don't assume equal variance. `car` can do this with what you already have loaded:

```r
Anova(fit, type = 2, white.adjust = "hc3")

emm_rob <- emmeans(fit, ~ approach, vcov. = hccm(fit, type = "hc3"))
confint(pairs(emm_rob))
```

**2. Weighted least squares / group-specific variances.** Model a separate residual variance for each approach using `gls()` from `nlme`, which ships with R:

```r
library(nlme)
fit_gls <- gls(qor15_30d ~ approach + age + bmi + diabetes,
               weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | approach),
               data = dat)
summary(fit_gls)
intervals(fit_gls)
anova(fit, fit_gls)  # won't work directly, since lm vs gls; refit the lm version with gls() to compare
```

`emmeans()` also works on `gls` objects.

**Some context for choosing.** OLS is fairly robust to unequal variances when the group sizes are **equal**, as yours are (100/100). The danger is greatest when the smaller group has the larger variance. Many people still report robust SEs as a sensitivity check. It can also help to look at the size of the difference, not just the p-value:

```r
dat %>% mutate(res = res) %>% group_by(approach) %>% summarise(sd_res = sd(res))
```

A ratio of residual SDs near 1 versus near 2 tells you more than whether $p < 0.05$, especially with $n = 200$, where small differences can reach significance.

Which approach to use, if any, is your call. Whatever you choose, state it and the reason in the assumptions section.
:::

confint(pairs(emmeans(fit, ~ approach, vcov. = hccm(fit, type = "hc3"))))
```

If the two versions agree, that's a strong one-sentence addition to your assumptions section. If they disagree, that's important to know too. Whether to include it is up to you.

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 39"}
Variances are on a squared scale, which makes differences look bigger than they are. It helps to put it as a ratio:

$$\frac{s^2_{\text{Lap}}}{s^2_{\text{Open}}} = \frac{175}{108} \approx 1.62, \qquad \frac{s_{\text{Lap}}}{s_{\text{Open}}} = \frac{13.2}{10.4} \approx 1.27$$

So the Laparoscopic group's residual SD is about 27% larger, or its variance about 1.6 times larger.

**Rules of thumb you'll see cited:**

- A largest-to-smallest **variance ratio under about 2** is commonly treated as minor; some sources tolerate up to about 3 or 4 when group sizes are equal.
- The robustness of OLS to unequal variances depends heavily on group sizes. With **equal $n$**, Type I error stays close to nominal even at fairly large ratios. The real trouble arises when the groups are unbalanced, especially when the *smaller* group has the *larger* variance.

These are heuristics, not hard cutoffs, and different textbooks draw the lines in different places. Whether 1.6 with 100/100 is acceptable is your judgment to state and defend. Citing the ratio and the balanced design together makes for a concrete argument.

If you want something firmer than a rule of thumb, that's what the HC3 sensitivity check is for. It directly shows whether the unequal variance changes your inference about approach in *this* dataset.
:::

Not quite. This is a **Q-Q plot**, which checks **normality of residuals**, not multicollinearity. It's the plot from `ggqqplot(res)`. VIF doesn't have a plot; it's just the numbers you already got (all about 1.0).

**Reading the Q-Q plot:**

- Each point is one residual. The x-axis shows where it *would* fall if the residuals were perfectly normal (theoretical quantiles), and the y-axis shows where it actually falls.
- If the residuals are normal, the points lie along the straight line.
- The grey band is a confidence envelope. Points within it are consistent with normality.

So yes, points following the line and staying inside the band is what you want to see. Things that would indicate a problem:

| Pattern | Suggests |
|---|---|
| Ends curve away in opposite directions (S-shape) | Heavy or light tails |
| Both ends bend the same way (banana shape) | Skewness |
| A few isolated points far off at the ends | Outliers |

Here the points track the line closely, with a slight wave in the middle that stays well within the band. That agrees with your Shapiro-Wilk result ($p = 0.96$). This plot plus that test makes a good pairing for the normality part of your assumptions section.

**For VIF in the report:** the usual interpretation is that values near 1 indicate essentially no collinearity, and concern typically starts around 5 or 10. Your values are all about 1.01 to 1.02. A small table works well:

kable(vif(fit), col.names = "VIF", digits = 2)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 45"}
For your final model, `fit` (no interaction terms), either type works. **Type II and Type III give identical tests for every term when there are no interactions.** The only visible difference is that Type III also prints an `(Intercept)` row, which you can ignore.

```r
Anova(fit, type = 2)
```

Type II is the conventional choice for an additive ANCOVA, but if you report Type III, the results will be the same.

**Background on the types:**

| Type | What it tests | When it matters |
|---|---|---|
| I (sequential), base `anova()` | Each term adjusted only for terms listed *before* it | Results depend on the order of terms in the formula, so it's usually not what you want for ANCOVA |
| II | Each term adjusted for all other terms, but not interactions involving it | Standard for models without interactions |
| III | Each term adjusted for everything, including interactions | Used when interactions are in the model; main effects then also depend on contrast coding |

So the main thing to avoid is base R's lowercase `anova(fit)` for the ANCOVA table, since it's sequential. Lowercase `anova(fit, fit_int)` for *comparing two models*, as you did for equal slopes, is fine.

The ANCOVA table gives you the test for approach. For the report's **effect sizes and confidence intervals**, pair it with:

```r
confint(pairs(emmeans(fit, ~ approach)))   # adjusted mean difference + 95% CI
eta_squared(fit, partial = TRUE)           # partial eta-squared
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Claude · turn 47"}
You're reading most of this correctly. Here's each piece, plus one code issue.

#### The ANCOVA table

Each row tests whether that term explains variation in QoR-15 **after adjusting for the other terms**.

- **Approach:** $F(1, 195) = 14.95$, $p = 0.00015$. This is the row that answers the study question.
- **Covariates:** age and diabetes are significant; BMI is at $p = 0.050$, just above 0.05.

One distinction worth thinking about as you write: approach was randomized, while age, BMI, and diabetes were observed. The covariate rows are tests of *adjusted associations* with QoR-15, which you may want to phrase differently from the treatment effect. How you phrase it is up to you.

#### Where the slopes are

The Anova table only gives sums of squares and tests, not the estimates. The slopes and differences are in the coefficient table:

```r
summary(fit)    # estimates, SEs, t-tests
confint(fit)    # 95% CIs for each coefficient
```

There you'll see, for example, the change in QoR-15 per year of age, holding other terms constant. The approach coefficient there should match the 6.62 from `emmeans` (possibly with the opposite sign, depending on your reference level).

#### The adjusted difference

Your reading is right: the adjusted mean QoR-15 was **6.62 points higher** for Laparoscopic than Open, with a 95% CI of **3.24 to 9.99**. The CI excludes 0, which matches the significant F-test.

The note "Results are averaged over the levels of: diabetes" means the adjusted means are computed with continuous covariates at their means and averaged across diabetes levels, so it's a covariate-adjusted comparison.

Whether that difference is small or meaningful is an interpretation call for you. One useful anchor: many instruments, including the QoR-15, have a published **minimal clinically important difference (MCID)**. Comparing your estimate and CI against an MCID from the literature is a standard way to judge practical significance, rather than eyeballing it against the 0–150 range.

#### Partial eta-squared: a code fix and a definition

**The fix:** notice the header says "**Type I**". `eta_squared()` on an `lm` object uses sequential sums of squares by default, so those values don't match your Type II table. Pass it the Type II table instead:

```r
eta_squared(Anova(fit, type = 2), partial = TRUE, alternative = "two.sided")
```

`alternative = "two.sided"` also gives a regular two-sided CI. The default one-sided CI with the upper bound fixed at 1.00 is why every row showed `1.00`.

**The definition:** your phrasing is close. Precisely,

$$\eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{\text{effect}}}{SS_{\text{effect}} + SS_{\text{residual}}}$$

In words, it's the proportion of variance attributable to that term, out of the variance *not explained by the other terms in the model*. For approach, about 7% of the variance remaining after age, BMI, and diabetes is attributable to approach.

You can verify it by hand from your table: $2141.0 / (2141.0 + 27930.6) \approx 0.071$.
:::
